title: PET, foil, polyethylene: how the layers in a laminate decide shelf life
excerpt: No single film prints well, blocks air and seals cleanly. A laminate gives each job to a different layer, and the choice of layers decides how long your product keeps.

image.alt: Three film layers peeled apart to show a laminate

children.text: Pick up almost any printed pouch and you are holding two or three films bonded into one sheet. It looks like a single material, but each layer is there for a different reason, and choosing them is the most important decision in a packaging job.
Why one film is not enough

A pack has to do three things: carry the print, protect the product and seal shut. No single plastic does all three well. Polyester prints beautifully but will not heat seal to itself. Polyethylene seals easily but stretches on the press and lets oxygen through. Aluminium foil blocks almost everything but tears and cannot be sealed at all. Lamination puts the three together so each one covers for the others.
The three jobs
The outer layer carries the print.
This is usually PET or BOPP: stiff, clear and stable under heat. The ink is printed on the inside face, so it ends up sandwiched between layers and cannot scuff or touch the product.
The middle layer is the barrier.
Aluminium foil, metallised PET or nylon sits here to keep out oxygen, moisture and light. Packs for products that are not sensitive can leave this layer out.
The inner layer makes the seal.

Polyethylene or cast polypropylene melts at a lower temperature than the outer layers, so the sealing jaws can weld the pouch shut without damaging the print. It is also the layer that touches the product.
Common structures and where they are used

cells: Bakery, stationery, dry goods with a short shelf life
Coffee, pharma powders, products with a long shelf life

children.text: Lamination adhesives can be solvent based or solventless. Solventless lamination leaves no residual smell, which is why it is the usual choice for food and pharmaceutical packs. Our
combi laminator
runs both.
What to tell your converter

You do not need to specify the structure yourself. Tell us what the product is, the fill weight, the shelf life you are aiming for, how the pack will be filled and how it will be stored and sold. From that we can propose a laminate and explain what each layer is doing in it.

title: Why a first order has a minimum and a repeat order costs less
excerpt: Gravure printing starts with engraved cylinders, one for every colour. They are the reason a first order has a floor, and the reason the second one is cheaper.

image.alt: An engraved gravure cylinder close up

children.text: New brands often ask why they cannot order five hundred printed pouches. The answer sits on a rack in the press room: a set of engraved metal cylinders that has to be made before a single pouch can be printed.
One cylinder for every colour

In rotogravure printing your artwork is engraved into the surface of a steel cylinder as millions of tiny cells. The cylinder turns through a tray of ink, a blade wipes the surface clean, and the ink left in the cells transfers to the film. Each colour in the design needs its own cylinder, so a nine-colour job needs nine.
Engraving is a fixed cost. It is the same whether you print five thousand pouches or five hundred thousand.
Why that creates a minimum

Two costs do not shrink with the order. The first is the cylinders. The second is make-ready: every job uses a length of film while the press is brought into register and the colours are matched to the approved shade. Spread over a large run, both are small. Spread over a very small run, they would cost more than the pouches themselves. The minimum order is simply the point at which the job makes sense for both sides.
Why the repeat is cheaper

Once the cylinders exist, they can be used again. A repeat order pays for film, ink and press time, but not for engraving. It also prints from the same cylinders as the first run, which is what keeps the colour consistent from one delivery to the next.

body.title: How we keep first runs small.

children.text: When several variants share a layout, we plan the artwork so that only one cylinder or one colour changes between them. That is how a new flavour can start at around 5,000 pouches on our
9-colour press
without a full new set of cylinders.
Three ways to bring your first order down
Share a layout across variants.
Keep the design common and change only the flavour name or a colour band.
Use fewer colours.
Every colour you remove is a cylinder you do not pay for.
Standardise the pouch size.
Variants in the same size can run together and share the set-up.
If you are planning a range,
talk to us before the design is final
. A small change at the artwork stage can take a meaningful amount off the first order.

title: Getting your artwork ready for nine gravure cylinders
excerpt: A design that looks right on screen still has to be separated, sized and checked before it can be engraved. Here is what our pre-press desk needs from you.

image.alt: Colour separations of a pouch design on a desk

children.text: Between the design your agency signs off and the pouch that comes off the line there is a step most brand owners never see. Pre-press turns a finished design into instructions for a set of cylinders. Getting the file right at this stage saves a round of corrections and, sometimes, the cost of re-engraving.
Send editable vector artwork

Logos, text and line work should be vector, not a flattened image, so that they stay sharp at any size and can be separated cleanly. Convert fonts to outlines or send the font files with the artwork. Photographs should be supplied at full resolution and linked, not pasted in at screen quality.
Think in inks, not in screen colours

Our press prints up to nine colours, and each one is a separate cylinder. Brand colours print best as their own mixed ink, so give a colour reference for each one and do not rely on how it looks on a monitor. On clear or metallised film a layer of white is usually printed behind the design so the colours stay opaque, and that white counts as one of the nine.
Keep clear of the seals

Part of every pouch is taken up by heat seals, and features such as a zipper, a tear notch or a hang hole take up more. Ask us for the keyline for your pouch size before the design starts. It shows where the seals, folds and fitments fall, so that no text or barcode ends up under a seal or across a gusset.
Small type and barcodes
Very small text
is safest in a single dark colour. Fine type built from several colours, or reversed out of a multi-colour background, depends on perfect register.
Thin lines and hairlines
can fill in or break up. Give them some weight.
Barcodes
need a dark bar on a light, solid background with clear space on both sides. Let us check the size and direction before engraving.
Our
artwork desk
separates the colours, sets the repeat length, adds the register marks the press and the pouching machine read, and sends you a proof. Nothing is engraved until you have approved it.
A short checklist
Editable vector file, fonts outlined
A colour reference for every brand colour
Pouch size, format and fitments confirmed
Barcode number and any statutory text supplied
One person named to approve the proof

title: Zipper, spout or valve: choosing the extras on a pouch
excerpt: The features added on the pouching line change how a pack is opened, poured, hung and closed again. A short guide to what each one is for.

image.alt: Pouches with a zipper, a spout, a valve and a hang hole

children.text: Two pouches made from the same laminate can behave very differently in a customer's hands. The difference is in the features added at the pouching stage. Each one solves a particular problem, and each adds a little cost, so it is worth choosing them on purpose.
For packs that are opened more than once
Zipper.
A press-to-close strip across the top lets the pouch be resealed. It suits anything used a little at a time: dry fruit, snacks, pulses, cereals.
Spout and cap.
A welded spout turns a pouch into a light, unbreakable alternative to a bottle for liquids and pastes. It pours cleanly and closes again.
For packs that are opened once
Tear notch.
A small cut in the side seal gives the customer a place to start tearing, so no scissors are needed.
Perforation.
A tear line between pouches in a string lets a shopkeeper hang a strip and sell it one pouch at a time. It is the standard pack for agarbatti.
For the shelf and the peg
Bottom gusset.
A fold in the base lets a pouch stand upright and face the shopper.
Euro punch or round punch.
A hole in the header lets the pack hang on a peg hook, which is how most stationery and electrical accessories are sold.
D-cut or loop handle.
A punched or attached handle for heavier packs and carry bags.
Window.
A clear, unprinted panel that lets the product sell itself.
For the product itself
Degassing valve.
Freshly roasted coffee gives off gas. A one-way valve lets it out without letting air in, so the pouch does not swell and the coffee stays fresh.

A zipper, a notch or a hang hole takes up space on the pouch, and the artwork has to leave room for it. Tell us which features you want before the design is finished. The full list of what we fit is on the
products page

title: What an anti-static pouch does for a circuit board
excerpt: Static that you cannot feel is enough to damage an electronic component. Anti-static film is made to carry that charge away before it builds up.

image.alt: A circuit board being slid into an anti-static pouch

children.text: Most packaging protects against things you can see: moisture, dust, knocks. Electronics need protection from something invisible. A static discharge far too small for a person to notice can damage a component, and the damage may not show until the product is in use.
Where the charge comes from

Static builds up whenever two materials rub together and separate. Ordinary plastic film is very good at this: a part sliding into a plain polyethylene bag, or two bags rubbing in a carton, generates charge. Because ordinary plastic does not conduct, the charge stays where it is until it finds something to jump to. If that something is a circuit board, the discharge passes through the components.
What anti-static film does differently

Anti-static film is made so that charge can spread across its surface and drain away slowly, and so that the film itself generates very little charge when it is rubbed. Nothing builds up, so there is nothing to discharge.
When you need it
Bare printed circuit boards and assembled boards
Loose components, modules and cartridges
Storage devices and anything with exposed contacts
Finished products in their own casing, such as switches, plugs and sockets, are usually packed in ordinary printed pouches. It is the exposed electronics that need the special film.

body.title: Static is not the only risk.

children.text: Some components are also sensitive to moisture. In that case anti-static film can be combined with a high barrier laminate. Both are described under
anti-static and high barrier pouches
What to tell us

Send the size of the part, whether it is a bare board or a cased product, how it is packed at your end, and whether it needs to be sealed or simply bagged. We make these pouches in three-side seal, centre seal, stand-up and zipper formats, plain or printed.

title: Roll stock or finished pouches: which should you order?
excerpt: The same printed laminate can leave our plant on a reel or as ready-made pouches. The right choice depends on how you fill your product.

image.alt: A reel of printed film beside a stack of finished pouches

children.text: Every job in our plant is printed and laminated in the same way. The difference comes at the end: some customers take the film as a reel, and some take it as finished pouches. Which one you need depends on what happens in your own factory.
Roll stock: for a form-fill-seal machine
If you own a machine that forms the pack, fills it and seals it in one pass, you buy film on the reel. Your order is finished at our
slitting stage
, where the wide printed roll is cut to the width your machine takes.
Roll stock usually costs less per pack, because the pouch-making step happens on your line and not on ours. In return, we need a few details about your machine before we start.
The film width and the repeat length of one pack
The core size and the largest reel your machine can carry
The winding direction, which decides which way the print faces as the film unwinds
The position of the register mark your machine reads
Finished pouches: for hand or semi-automatic filling
If your product is filled by hand, by a weigher or on a simple band sealer, you buy ready-made pouches. They arrive formed and sealed on three sides, and you fill and close the fourth.
Pouches are also the only route to features that a basic filling machine cannot add: a zipper, a spout, a stand-up base, a custom shape.

children.text: Many brands start with finished pouches and move to roll stock when the volume justifies a machine. The cylinders made for the pouch can often be reused if the pack size stays the same, so tell us early if that is the plan.

detailsCopy: A spice needs a laminate that keeps moisture out for months. A printed circuit board needs a film that bleeds away static. A box of pencils needs a clear, stiff bag with a hole that hangs straight on a peg. The sector decides the structure, and the structure decides which machine the job runs on.
Tell us the product, the fill weight and how it will be sold, and we will propose a laminate, a format and a quantity to start with.

seo.title: Infrastructure | Printing, lamination, slitting and pouching | Spectra Pack
seo.description: Inside the Umbergaon plant: 9-colour rotogravure printing, combi lamination, slitting, three pouching lines and an in-house quality lab.

title: A converting plant *in Umbergaon*

image.alt: The production floor seen along a printing press

artworkText: Bring your finished design. Our in-house artwork desk prepares it for the press, so that what you approved on screen is what comes off the cylinders.

artworkImage.alt: A pre-press operator checking a pouch layout on screen

artworkChecklist.title: Colour separation
artworkChecklist.text: Your artwork is split into up to nine inks, one cylinder for each.

artworkChecklist.title: Variant planning
artworkChecklist.text: Flavours and sizes that share a layout are planned as single-cylinder or single-colour changes.

artworkChecklist.title: Shade matching
artworkChecklist.text: Inks are mixed to your approved shade and matched again on every repeat order.

processLead: Every machine in the 27,000 sq ft plant does something to a long reel of thin film. The film goes in plain and comes out printed, thicker, narrower, or folded into a bag. Here are the four steps, and the machines that run each one.

steps.title: Printing
steps.text: Your artwork is engraved into metal cylinders. Each cylinder turns through one ink and presses it onto the film, one colour at a time, up to nine colours. The method is called rotogravure.
steps.why: Engraving the cylinders is the costly part of a first order, which is why it carries a minimum quantity. When a variant shares the layout, we change a single cylinder or a single colour instead of the whole set, so a run of 5,000 pouches stays affordable.

image.alt: Film passing over an inked gravure cylinder

steps.title: Lamination
steps.text: Two or three different films are bonded into one sheet. A typical build is PET, aluminium foil and polyethylene: the outside carries the print, the middle blocks light and air, and the inside melts to form the seal.
steps.why: The choice of layers decides how long your product keeps. Solventless lamination leaves no odour, which is what food and pharmaceutical packs need.

image.alt: Two films meeting at a lamination nip roller

steps.title: Slitting
steps.text: The wide printed roll is cut lengthways into narrower reels, each one sized to the machine that will run it next.
steps.why: If you form and fill on your own line, this is where your order is finished. You receive reels, not pouches.

image.alt: A wide roll being slit into narrower reels

steps.title: Pouching
steps.text: The film is folded and heat sealed into a finished bag, and the extras are added: a zipper, a spout and cap, a hang hole, a tear notch, or a one-way valve for coffee.
steps.why: Three pouching lines cover three-side and centre seal, side seal, and bottom seal formats, so most jobs have a machine suited to them.

image.alt: Finished pouches coming off a pouching machine

qualityText: Film is tested when it arrives, while it runs and before it leaves. The in-house lab checks each job against the product it will carry, and a certificate of analysis can travel with the consignment.

qualityImage.alt: A seal strength test in the quality lab

qualityChecklist.title: Seal strength and tensile tests
qualityChecklist.text: Confirms that the pouch holds under the weight and handling it will meet.

qualityChecklist.title: Friction (COF), static and kinetic
qualityChecklist.text: Confirms that the film will run cleanly on a filling machine.

qualityChecklist.title: Thickness, oven and compression tests
qualityChecklist.text: Micrometers, a hot-air oven and a compression tester check the laminate itself.

qualityChecklist.title: Inspection of every printed roll
qualityChecklist.text: The doctoring machine stops on a misprint so that it is cut out before pouching.

seo.title: Privacy policy | Spectra Pack
seo.description: How Spectra Pack collects, uses and protects personal information sent through this website.

children.text: This policy explains what personal information Spectra Pack collects through this website, why we collect it, and the choices you have. We have tried to keep it short and in plain language.
Who we are

This website is run by Spectra Pack, a manufacturer of flexible packaging, at A-1/503, GIDC Road, Phase 3, GIDC Umbergaon, Umargam, Gujarat 396171, India. In this policy "we", "us" and "our" mean Spectra Pack. You can reach us about anything in this policy at
info@spectrapack.co.in
What we collect
Information you choose to send us.

When you send the enquiry form, we receive the details you entered: your name, company, email address, phone number and, if you add them, your country, industry, the product you are interested in, the quantity and your message. The form is delivered through Netlify, the company that hosts this website, which keeps the submission in a password-protected account and emails it to our sales team. We also receive whatever you share when you call us, email us or message us on WhatsApp.
Information collected automatically.

This website does not set its own cookies and does not use analytics or advertising trackers. Like any website, the server that hosts it may keep standard technical logs, such as your IP address, browser type and the pages requested, for security and to keep the site running.
Services run by other companies.
Some parts of the site are provided by third parties, who receive basic technical information such as your IP address when your browser loads them:
Netlify
, which hosts this website and receives enquiry form submissions on our behalf.
Sanity
, which stores the text and images of this website and delivers the images to your browser.
Google Fonts
, which supplies the typeface used on every page.
Google Maps
, which shows our location on the contact page. Google may set its own cookies when the map loads.
WhatsApp, Instagram and Google Maps links.
If you follow these links, you leave our site and the other service's own privacy policy applies.
How we use your information
To reply to your enquiry and prepare a quotation.
To process, deliver and support any order you place with us.
To keep business records that the law requires us to keep, such as tax and accounting records.
We do not sell your personal information, and we do not send you marketing messages unless you have asked to receive them.
Why we are allowed to use it

We process the information you send us with your consent, which you give by contacting us, and so that we can respond to a request you have made. You can withdraw your consent at any time by writing to us. Withdrawing it does not affect anything we did with your information before you withdrew it.
Who we share it with

Your information is seen by the people at Spectra Pack who need it to answer you. It is also handled by the providers we rely on to run our business, such as our email provider and Netlify, our website host, only for that purpose. We may disclose information where the law requires it. We do not share it with anyone for their own marketing.
How long we keep it
We keep enquiry correspondence for as long as it is useful for the enquiry or for an ongoing business relationship, and business records for as long as the law requires. After that we delete it.
Your rights
Under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, you can ask us:
for a summary of the personal information we hold about you and how we use it;
to correct, complete or update it;
to erase it, where we no longer need it or you withdraw consent;
to nominate another person to exercise these rights on your behalf.
To make a request, write to
info@spectrapack.co.in
. We will reply within a reasonable time. If you are not satisfied with our reply, you may complain to the Data Protection Board of India.
Keeping it safe

We take reasonable steps to protect the information you send us from loss and from unauthorised access. No method of sending or storing information over the internet is completely secure, so please do not send us sensitive information, such as bank or identity documents, through the enquiry form.
Children
This website is meant for businesses and is not directed at children. We do not knowingly collect information from anyone under 18.
Changes to this policy
If we change this policy, we will publish the new version on this page and update the date at the top.
For questions or complaints about your personal information, write to
info@spectrapack.co.in
or to Spectra Pack, A-1/503, GIDC Road, Phase 3, GIDC Umbergaon, Umargam, Gujarat 396171, India.
